title: Map your terrain
summary: Identify situations that recur in your observations.

states.title: Times and states
states.paragraph1: Time and place can become recurring context cues. Stress, boredom, or trying to get some distance from a difficult emotion may also appear in your observations.
states.paragraph2: An experience-sampling study found that everyday desires are frequent and often tied to what the person is doing at the time. Feeling regular urges is therefore not, in itself, a sign of a problem.
states.paragraph3: Treat these repetitions as hypotheses, not causes: several observations over time are more informative than one coincidence.
states.keyPoint1: Record the time, place, and state—not the content.
states.keyPoint2: Look for a pattern across several days.
states.keyPoint3: A frequent urge is not a diagnosis.

motives.title: The reasons behind use
motives.paragraph1: A study of use motivations identified several very different ones: sexual pleasure, curiosity, boredom, fantasy, stress reduction, or avoiding an emotion.
motives.paragraph2: In that work, several motives related to managing difficulty—reducing stress, distracting from an emotion, or responding to boredom—were associated with problematic use, as were fantasy and sexual pleasure. All of these associations remained weak to moderate.
motives.paragraph3: Identifying your dominant motive changes the rest of the plan: repeated boredom does not call for the same response as a stressful evening or a lonely moment.

routines.title: Devices and routines
routines.paragraph1: A device available in the same place and at the same time can make an automatic response easier.
routines.paragraph2: Habit-formation research shows that repetition in a stable context strengthens automaticity, with wide differences between people and behaviors: there is no fixed number of days after which a habit is simply “set”.
routines.paragraph3: If your notes show that social media or an evening routine often comes first, treat it as a useful pattern—not necessarily the only cause.

emotions.title: Emotions as a marker
emotions.paragraph1: Naming the emotion present just before an impulse often carries more information than naming the impulse itself.
emotions.paragraph2: A meta-analysis covering emotion regulation and symptoms of anxiety, depression, eating, and substance-related disorders observes that avoidance and suppression strategies are associated with more difficulties, while problem solving and reappraisal are associated with fewer.
emotions.paragraph3: These findings describe group tendencies. They do not mean your way of coping is at fault: they mainly suggest widening the range of responses available to you.
emotions.keyPoint1: Name the emotion before judging the behavior.
emotions.keyPoint2: Widening your responses beats banning one of them.
emotions.keyPoint3: Three words are enough: when, where, which state.

map.title: A map, not a verdict
map.paragraph1: Mapping your terrain helps you prepare options. It does not mean avoiding every difficult situation.
map.paragraph2: A map with too much detail can become hard to use. You can start with two or three recurring situations to build a realistic plan.
map.paragraph3: A few general observations are enough; no explicit detail or browsing history is useful.

reflectionPrompt: Which situation appears most often in your observations?
